header.label: OpenAEC Ecosystem
header.title: Software architecture
header.desc: One codebase, all platforms. Our tools run as a web app, as a desktop application on Windows, Linux and macOS, and as a mobile app — from the same source code.

intro.title: One codebase, everywhere
intro.p1: Every tool in the OpenAEC ecosystem is developed as a single application that runs on all platforms. No separate versions for web and desktop, no double maintenance. The same code, the same features, everywhere.
intro.p2: Our starting point is Rust. We prefer to build full Rust applications, with the interface written in Rust as well. Sometimes we choose Tauri with a TypeScript frontend on a Rust core, for example when a tool also has to run in the browser.

tech.title: Technology stack
tech.tauri_desc: Framework for building desktop and mobile apps with web technology. Uses the native webview of the OS instead of Chromium — resulting in small installation files (<10MB) and low memory usage.
tech.rust_desc: The core logic of every tool is written in Rust: IFC parsing, validation, calculations and file processing. Rust offers memory safety, high performance and compiles to every platform.
tech.wasm_desc: The same Rust code compiles to WebAssembly (WASM) for the web version. This allows the full computation logic to also run in the browser, with near-native performance.
tech.ui_desc: In a full Rust app the interface is Rust too. Where we use Tauri, we build the interface with TypeScript (React, Svelte or SolidJS) and Vite; it then runs in Tauri and in the browser.
tech.threejs_desc: 3D visualization of IFC models via Three.js and That Open Engine. WebGL-based, runs everywhere a browser runs.
tech.fastapi_desc: Server-side APIs built with Python FastAPI for async validation, document management and integrations. Deployed via Docker.

highlight.title: Local and in the cloud — one system
highlight.desc: Every OpenAEC tool works standalone on your own machine, without an internet connection. But when you connect, everything synchronizes seamlessly with the cloud via the OpenAEC platform. Projects, documents and model data flow automatically between local installations and the server. You choose: fully local, fully in the cloud, or a hybrid setup.

extensibility.title: Extensibility & integration
extensibility.desc: The tools are designed to be extended and connected. Four ways, which differ per tool:
extensibility.feedback_desc: A feedback button in the app, as in Open Safety Studio and Open 3D Viewer. Users report bugs and wishes straight from the application.
extensibility.api_desc: Tools with a server, such as BIM Validator, BCF Manager Studio and OpenAEC Docs, offer a REST API. Connect them to your own systems or dashboards.
extensibility.mcp_desc: Model Context Protocol (MCP), among others in Open Pointcloud Studio. It lets AI agents (like Claude) operate the tool directly through natural language.
extensibility.extensions_desc: Tools such as Open 2D Studio support extensions for custom work, for example Drawing Statistics. Build your own plugins in TypeScript or Rust.

opensource.title: Building on existing open source projects
opensource.desc: We don't reinvent the wheel. The OpenAEC ecosystem builds as much as possible on proven open source projects from the BIM and 3D world:
opensource.thatopen_desc: The 3D rendering and IFC parsing in our viewers is based on That Open Engine (formerly IFC.js). A powerful TypeScript/Three.js library for BIM in the browser.
opensource.blender_desc: For 3D modeling and BIM authoring we integrate with Blender and the Bonsai add-on (formerly BlenderBIM). The most powerful open source 3D tool in the world.
opensource.ifcopenshell_desc: The industry-standard Python/C++ library for reading, writing and manipulating IFC files. The backbone of our server-side IFC processing.
opensource.pdfjs_desc: Mozilla's PDF.js for rendering and pdf-lib for programmatically creating and editing PDF documents. Proven technology, millions of users.

why.title: Why this approach?
why.small_desc: No Electron, no Chromium. A full Rust app needs no webview at all, and Tauri uses the webview that is already part of the operating system. Installers stay small and memory use stays low.
why.safe_desc: Rust prevents memory errors, buffer overflows and race conditions. The application is secure by design.
why.opensource_desc: Tauri, Rust, and all libraries used are open source. No vendor lock-in at framework level.
why.futureproof_desc: Web standards and Rust are technologies with long lifespans. No framework churn, no breaking changes.

extensibility.desc: Every tool in the ecosystem is designed to be extended and integrated. Four layers of extensibility:
extensibility.feedback_desc: Built-in feedback system in every tool. Users can provide feedback, report bugs and submit feature requests directly from the application. Connected to the central platform.
extensibility.api_desc: Every tool offers a REST API for integration with external systems. Automate workflows, connect with ERP systems or build your own dashboards on top of the ecosystem.
extensibility.mcp_desc: Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers for every tool. This allows AI agents (like Claude) to communicate directly with the tools — validate models, generate documents or perform calculations via natural language.
extensibility.extensions_desc: Every tool supports extensions for custom functionality. Build your own plugins in TypeScript or Rust and share them with the community via the extension registry.

routes.title: Rust first, Tauri where it fits
routes.lead: We prefer to build full Rust applications. For some tools we deliberately choose Tauri with a TypeScript interface on a Rust core.

rust.title: Full Rust
rust.desc: Computation core and user interface in Rust, as a single native program. No webview and no JavaScript: fast start-up, little memory and one language for the whole codebase.
rust.li1: For heavy, graphical tools: CAD, BIM and large models
rust.li2: The same Rust core can also run in the browser through WebAssembly

tauri.title: Tauri + TypeScript
tauri.desc: A Rust core with an interface in TypeScript, in the operating system’s webview. The same interface then also runs as a web app in the browser.
tauri.li1: For tools that must also work in the browser, or that mostly show forms and documents
tauri.li2: The computation stays in Rust; TypeScript only does the interface
